title: Which digits hide behind the letters in six puzzles?
description: Six letter puzzles with multiplication are solved one after another, the way the book's solved examples do it. Each puzzle is cut down first by the number of digits in its answer, then by the last digit, and then the few choices left are tried. Every answer is put back into its puzzle to check.
teaching_notes: One idea: use the number of digits in the answer to bound the numbers, use the last digits to narrow the choices, and test what is left. Watch for students who guess digits without checking the size of the answer.

source: Digits in Disguise: solve the six
video_script.why: The child can multiply, and now uses units digits and the size of numbers to crack letter puzzles.
video_script.substitution: Fix the units digit first, then use the count of digits to bound the rest.
video_script.anchor: the six letter multiplication puzzles of the book: UT × 3 = PUT, AB × 5 = BC, L2N × 2 = 2NP, XY × 4 = ZX, PP × QQ = PRP and JK × 6 = KKK
video_script.payoff_line: Fifty times three is one hundred and fifty.

final_answer.spoken: fifty times three is one hundred and fifty, nineteen times five is ninety five, one hundred and twenty four times two is two hundred and forty eight or one hundred and twenty five times two is two hundred and fifty, twenty three times four is ninety two, twenty two, thirty three or forty four times eleven, and seventy four times six is four hundred and forty four

maths_rules: (i) UT × 3 = PUT: 3 × T ends in T, so T is 0 or 5; T = 5 gives carry 1 and 3 × U + 1 is odd, so it cannot end in U; T = 0 needs 3 × U to end in U, so U = 5 (U is not 0); 50 × 3 = 150, P = 1
(ii) AB × 5 = BC has two digits, so AB is at most 19 and A = 1; 5 × (10 + B) = 50 + 5B must have tens digit B; only B = 9 works, 19 × 5 = 95, C = 5

(iii) L2N × 2 = 2NP: the answer is under 300, so L2N is under 150 and L = 1; 2 × 2 + carry = N, so N = 4 (no carry, 2 × 4 = 8) or N = 5 (carry 1, 2 × 5 = 10); 124 × 2 = 248 (P = 8), 125 × 2 = 250 (P = 0)
(iv) XY × 4 = ZX has two digits, so XY is at most 24; 4 × Y is even and ends in X, so X = 2; 4 × Y ends in 2 for Y = 3 or 8; 28 is too big; 23 × 4 = 92, Z = 9

(v) PP × QQ = 11P × 11Q = 121 × P × Q; three digits needs P × Q at most 8; the last digit is P × Q and must be P, so Q = 1; P = 1 repeats Q; P = 5 or more gives 121 × P with the wrong first digit; 22 × 11 = 242, 33 × 11 = 363, 44 × 11 = 484
video_script.design: Six puzzles in the book's order. Each is cut by the size of its answer, narrowed by the last digit, and the few cases left are tried. The check puts the answers back.

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step one, take U T times three equals P U T. Three times T ends in T, so T is zero or five.
<bookmark mark='five'/>T as five fails, because three times U plus one cannot end in U.
<bookmark mark='zero'/>T as zero needs U as five, so U T is fifty.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Next take eigh B times five equals B C. The answer has two digits, so eigh B is at most nineteen.
<bookmark mark='nineteen'/>The answer starts with B, and only nineteen fits.

narration: <bookmark mark='third'/>Step two, take L two N times two equals two N P. The answer is under three hundred, so L is one.
<bookmark mark='tens'/>N is four plus the carry, so N is four or five.
<bookmark mark='n4'/>One hundred and twenty four times two is two hundred and forty eight.
<bookmark mark='n5'/>One hundred and twenty five times two is two hundred and fifty.
<bookmark mark='fourth'/>Next take X Y times four equals Z X. X Y is at most twenty four.
<bookmark mark='x'/>Four times Y is even and ends in X, so X is two.
<bookmark mark='y'/>Y is three or eight, and twenty eight is too big.

narration: <bookmark mark='fifth'/>Step three, take P P times Q Q equals P R P. P P is eleven times P, and Q Q is eleven times Q.
<bookmark mark='all'/>Together they give one hundred and twenty one times P times Q.
<bookmark mark='size'/>Three digits need P times Q to be at most eight.
<bookmark mark='last'/>The last digit is P times Q, and it must be P. That makes Q equal to one.
<bookmark mark='p'/>P is not one, and P as five or more makes the answer too big.
<bookmark mark='three'/>That leaves P as two, three or four.

<bookmark mark='even'/>K must be even.
<bookmark mark='a'/>K as two gives thirty seven, and K as four gives seventy four.
<bookmark mark='b'/>K as six gives one hundred and eleven, and K as eight gives a three digit number.
<bookmark mark='only'/>Only seventy four ends in K, which is four.
